# Project Instructions

This workspace supports preparation of an EB1A RFE response, including organizing evidence and drafting supporting materials. Follow these instructions for all work in the project.

## Accuracy and Evidence

- Treat user-provided documents and primary sources as authoritative. Do not invent facts, dates, citation counts, credentials, quotations, or legal requirements.
- Keep factual statements traceable to a source. Flag missing, conflicting, or unverified information instead of filling gaps with assumptions.
- Preserve the meaning of source documents when summarizing or editing. Clearly distinguish source facts from proposed wording, analysis, and open questions.
- Do not describe assistance as legal advice or make guarantees about USCIS outcomes. Keep legal conclusions and filing decisions with the user's attorney.

## Independent Citation Record

- Follow `Independent Citation Record/Independent Citation Record Guide.md` when preparing citation-record materials.
- Use the user's Google Scholar profile as the primary source for citation totals and citing-paper lists, consistent with the guide. Record the source URL and dated snapshot for any figures reported.
- A citation is independent only when the citing paper and cited paper share no authors. Verify author lists before classifying a citation; do not infer independence from title or institution alone.
- Per the user's instruction, papers authored by the PI (Richard D. Cummings) or the former PI (Umesh R. Desai) are self-citations and are never counted as independent, even on papers that the user did not co-author.
- "Desai" and "Cummings" are common surnames. Match authors on surname plus initials, never surname alone. When surnames collide but initials are unavailable for comparison, flag the entry for manual review instead of counting or excluding it.
- Google Scholar truncates author lists with an ellipsis. Resolve the full list from Google Scholar itself: the cited paper's profile article page (`#gsc_oci_table`) and, for citing entries, the BibTeX record behind that result's "Cite" control. Do not substitute CrossRef or another third-party database as the primary basis for independence.
- **Scholar's BibTeX is itself abbreviated**, with `and others`, on long papers — so "we read the Cite popup" is not by itself a complete list. The capture records that case honestly as `full_authors` populated **and** `truncated = true`, with `resolution = "resolved but Scholar shows 'and others'"`. Measured 2026-11-03: 196 active rows have both, and all 19 queued rows that have a BibTeX list are of this abbreviated kind. What keeps an abbreviated list off an exhibit is the corroboration stage, which derives `confirm_state` from `!truncated` and demotes an incomplete INDEPENDENT to REVIEW — **not** `name-match.evaluateEntry`, which returns INDEPENDENT whenever `full_authors` is non-empty without consulting `truncated`. Verified 2026-11-03 that **0 highlighted rows** rest on an abbreviated list without a complete external or human basis. Reordering those two branches is **not** a no-op — it changes the intermediate status of 534 of 4021 entries — so it is a rule change to discuss with the user, not a cleanup. `popup_sample` is kept to 400 chars, so `and others` usually cannot be re-derived from the saved sample; read `resolution` instead.
- Per the user's instruction, corroborate each candidate independent citation against an external record that publishes the complete author list (PubMed via NCBI E-utilities, then OpenAlex) before highlighting it. Google Scholar stays primary. Record the external source and link. A paper indexed in neither service may still be highlighted when Scholar's own list is complete, but flag it for a spot-check.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, an external record settles a row rather than merely shadowing it: where a complete external author list shares an author with the cited paper or lists either PI, the row is dependent, and where it shares nobody it clears a Scholar byline that the page truncated. This supersedes the earlier rule that an external disagreement only downgraded a row to manual review and that no entry was ever promoted on an external record alone. Both transitions live in one place, `tools/corroboration.js`, called by the live capture and by `tools/reapply-corroboration.js` — never reimplement the state change in either caller.
- Believe an external record only when it is the same work. A title match must clear a credibility test before it can set a row's state (`titleMatchIsCredible` in `tools/crosscheck.js`): about 80% of the longer title's words, or a shorter side of at least four words wholly contained, or a leading prefix of at least **three** words, since Scholar truncates a long title with an ellipsis. Never accept a match on a one- or two-word fragment — a lone surname, an instrument acronym, or a journal name Scholar mistook for a title will match an unrelated paper. The prefix floor was two until 2026-11-02, which re-admitted exactly that class: `"[CITATION] Structural Biology"` matched the unrelated `"Structural biology of allergens"`. Measured over the settled corpus the raise to three costs nothing — only three rows rested on a prefix and all three had three words or more. Discarding an invalid match is not a policy change: it removes evidence that was never valid and the row falls back to whatever Scholar's own list supports, with `external_match_credible = 0` recorded and any byline the bad match overwrote restored to Scholar's own.
- Google Scholar prefixes some citing rows with a bracketed link-type marker — `[CITATION]`, `[BOOK]`, `[TXT]`. It is part of Scholar's rendering and **not part of the title**, and it is never evidence of anything about the work itself: not of a preprint, not of a non-English entry, and not of being unindexed. Stripping it happens in one place, `tools/scholar-marker.js`, used by the external look-up string and by `paperKey`. Leaving it in was the artifact behind most of the "Nothing indexes it" bucket: the word "citation" travelled into the PubMed and OpenAlex query, so no record could ever match. Only a leading marker on the allowlist is removed — a chemistry title's own brackets, as in `"...Benzopyrano[4,3-e][1,2,4]triazolo..."`, are the compound name and must survive.
- A look-up that did not complete is **not** a finding that a paper is unindexed. Throttled or failed requests used to fall through to `unverified-coverage`, which is a settling state, so an OpenAlex rate limit silently manufactured countable evidence. `tools/crosscheck.js` now retries 429 and 5xx honouring `Retry-After` and reports `{ unknown: true }`; `capture-citations.js` files that outcome as `confirm_state = 'lookup-failed'`, which is deliberately **not** settling, and demotes an INDEPENDENT row back to REVIEW. `tools/refetch-corroboration.js` exits non-zero when any look-up failed, so a throttled sweep fails loudly instead of quietly settling rows — re-run it until it exits 0 rather than accepting a partial pass.
- Honour `Retry-After` only up to a ceiling (`RETRY_MAX_WAIT_MS`, 60s in `tools/crosscheck.js`); beyond it, abandon the row as an incomplete look-up. Waiting a hint literally is not a retry: the anonymous OpenAlex pool answered `Retry-After: 44969` (~12.5h) on 2026-11-03 and the sweep sat in one sleep emitting pacing lines, indistinguishable from a slow run. Abandoning is the honest outcome because the caller leaves the row alone and fails loudly.
- Credentials for the external look-ups live in `.env` at the repository root (git-ignored; `.env.example` is the tracked template) and are loaded by `tools/env.js` at require time, so a key never has to appear on a command line where it would land in shell history or a recorded scrollback. A variable already set in the real environment wins. **An OpenAlex key is effectively required**, not optional: the anonymous pool throttles a corroboration sweep into a twelve-hour wait, while the same request with a key returns 200.
- Send an OpenAlex key as an `Authorization: Bearer` header, **never** as an `api_key` query parameter, even though both are accepted. `getJson` records a failed request as `${msg} :: ${url}` and that note can be written into a report JSON that ships in the evidence folder, so a credential in a URL would be filed with it. Never log a credential value anywhere; `crosscheck.credentialSummary()` prints the names in play only, and a run logs it at start and warns when no OpenAlex key is present.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **a re-look-up targets the review queue and nothing else** — `refetch-corroboration.js` scopes to `tally.isReviewQueue` by default, so it never re-queries a row the packet has already settled. This is right on the merits, not merely smaller: a queued row is undecided so new evidence can only resolve it, while a counted row is filed evidence whose mark a fresh query could silently change. Measured the same day, the old default (marker rows, any status) reached 58 rows of which **34 were already highlighted**, and an earlier such run moved the packet total from 1047 to 1049 independent — a sweep that can move a filed figure is not a cleanup. Widening still exists (`--widen=marker`, `--widen=unindexed`, since the marker bug did affect counted rows) but each prints a warning naming that counted rows are in scope. `--all-unindexed` remains as the old spelling of `--widen=unindexed`.
- External author names are normalised to natural order at look-up time (`toDisplayName` in `tools/crosscheck.js`). PubMed returns "Surname, Given" and the list is stored as one comma-joined string, so an inverted name tore into a phantom bare surname plus a given name — 21 of 692 rows, and it flipped a correctly DEPENDENT row to REVIEW when the phantom surname collided with a real author. Never reassemble a stored byline by guessing where a comma belongs; `--repair-names` re-reads an affected row from the service instead. Of those 21 rows only one is still classified REVIEW and none is on the queue, so repairing them cannot move a filed figure — re-derive the set with a read-only query against the store, and `tornAuthors` is the detector.
- A **discarded** external match (`external_match_credible = 0`) keeps its `external_source` as the audit trail of the rejection but its URL is never published. The link points at a different paper — cit-001476's PubMed hit is a swine-lung article that scored 0.07 against a `Glycoproteomics` byline — and the dashboard JSON ships with the packet, so hiding it at render time while the data still carries it is not enough. `externalUrl(r)` in `tools/build-dashboard-data.js` is the one gate, applied to every projection out of the store (`review_queue`, `allWorks`, `language_held`/unsettled), and `tools/build-review-sheet.js` blanks the same column. Adding a new listing means routing through that helper, not reading `external_url` directly.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, a row the rules cannot settle is resolved by a person through `tools/apply-decision.js` (`--row=cit-000082 --verdict=dependent --write --reprint --rebuild`, or fill `your_decision` in the review CSV and pass `--from-csv`). A human decision is its own basis, `confirm_state = 'user-decided'`, reported separately as "settled by you" and never folded into "externally confirmed", so a packet figure can state how much of it rests on a person's reading. `tally.js` treats it as settling a row, and `copyReliability` ranks a decided copy of a duplicated paper above any machine reading.
- A decision is written into the per-page report JSON and the store is rebuilt from it; never `UPDATE` `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` to record one, since the next `tools/build-catalog.js` silently reverts it and a store that disagrees with the reports is the state `tools/build-ledger.js` exits non-zero on. `apply-decision.js` resolves the `row_uid` against the store, locates the entry in its report, and refuses the whole batch unless the title at that position matches — editing a citation nobody asked about is worse than refusing. It is dry-run by default, backs up what it touches to `Exhibits/Supporting/Pre-decision-<date>/`, writes atomically, and `--revert` restores the exact pre-decision state. It does not re-fetch from Scholar: the user's reading of the published article is the evidence, and `decided_by`/`decided_on`/`decided_note` record who and why.
- A decision cannot override the language screen. Per the 2026-11-01 no-translation decision, classifying a non-English row as independent leaves it unhighlighted and out of the totals; the tool says so rather than letting the user infer it from a total that did not move.
- Keep citation counts and percentages tied to a dated Google Scholar snapshot. Identify the source and snapshot date whenever reporting totals.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-10-30, independent and dependent counts must be kept in a log usable for both per-article and global statistics. Run `tools/build-ledger.js` after every batch and quote figures from `Exhibits/Supporting/citation-ledger-<snapshot>.csv` (and its `.json`) rather than recomputing them; each run also appends a line to `citation-ledger-history.csv`. Do not maintain a parallel tally: `tools/tally.js` holds the single definition of what counts, and a publication contributes only while its exhibit PDF is filed.
- PENDING USER CONFIRMATION (2026-11-02 — a wording change to the bullet above, flagged rather than quietly applied): the bullet still stands, quote from the dated CSV and never recompute by hand. What changed is which artifact holds the rows. `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` is the primary durable store of the citation rows and must not be deleted; `tools/build-ledger.js` reads the active rows out of it and its CSV is a **derived report** of those rows, while still recomputing the same figures independently from the report JSON as a cross-check. A disagreement between the two is a defect to investigate, is resolved in neither side's favour, and both tools exit non-zero and write nothing — so do not quote any figure from a run that failed, and do not "fix" it by picking the number you prefer.
- Refer to a citation row by its `row_uid` (`cit-000106`), never by the integer `id`. The uid is minted once, never reused, and still means the same row after a re-capture or a rebuild; `id` is a frozen legacy alias. Every listing from `tools/query-catalog.js` leads with it. A row whose exhibit is archived or re-captured is retired with `superseded_at` and a reason, never deleted, and `tools/build-catalog.js` merges into the store rather than replacing it — run it without `--write` first to see the plan.
- `Database/Backups/` holds the verified pre-write snapshots the builder takes. Keep them on disk as the recovery path; do not commit them (they are several megabytes each and a new one appears on nearly every run) and do not delete them to save space. The tracked durable copy is `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite` itself.
- For non-English citations, do not treat machine translation as certified. Follow the guide's requirement for a human translator fluent in both languages and an accompanying certification/affidavit; otherwise exclude those entries from highlighted and adjusted English-only totals.
- Per the user's decision on 2026-11-01, no translations will be obtained. Non-English entries stay unhighlighted and the packet reports an adjusted independent total and percentage based solely on English citations, which is the guide's second path. The guide's test is whether an entry is "listed in English", meaning its title, author list and venue, not its body — so a foreign-language abstract under an English title is not evidence of a non-English entry.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, a non-English entry is **not on the review queue** — it belongs in the Non-English listing only (`cit-000077` was the example). The queue is the list where reading the published byline settles something, and with no translations being obtained no reading of such a row can change the packet, so it is not work. The single definition is `isReviewQueue` in `tools/tally.js` (`status === 'REVIEW'` and no language flag); `v_review`, `v_pub_stats`, `tools/build-ledger.js`, `tools/build-review-sheet.js`, `tools/query-catalog.js` and the dashboard all mirror that one condition. Keep both figures: `review` counts every REVIEW row so the status partition still sums to `records`, while `review_queue` is the sheet length — today 72 and 67. Never delete the excluded count; it stays in `review_non_english`, in `flagged_non_english`, and in `v_non_english`.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **the language screen supersedes a row's other classifications**: "if language is non-english that should supersede any other flags like independent … we should collapse them into non-English." So `isIndependentPending` in `tools/tally.js` requires no language flag, and a non-English row is reported once, under the non-English bucket, never as unsettled independent work. This is the same reasoning as the queue rule above applied to the INDEPENDENT rows: with no certified translations being obtained, no reading of a byline changes the packet, so calling those rows "unsettled" overstated the remaining work. Measured the same day, all 45 rows the dashboard had labelled "Independent but unsettled" were non-English — 42 withheld by the screen and 3 second-language copies of one German article whose English version is already highlighted (`cit-000991`, `cit-001260`, `cit-001539`) — and **0** were genuinely open.
- Collapsing them does not remove them from the status partition. `tally.js` publishes `non_english_independent` (45) for the rows that carry an INDEPENDENT classification and are held by the language screen, because `tallyEntries` and the per-article gate in `tools/check-ledger-vs-snapshot.js` must still sum to `records`: `independent + independent_pending + non_english_independent + secondary_copy_independent + dependent + self + review = records`. It is **not** the same set as `non_english_withheld` (42), which additionally requires a settled basis and excludes language editions because it answers "what would a translator reclaim" — do not merge the two figures. Adding the term means touching `build-ledger.js` (both row builders, the totals seed, `CSV_COLUMNS`, the global block), `build-catalog.js` `reconcile()`, `query-catalog.js` `stats()` and `build-dashboard-data.js`; a store SQL that stops matching the predicate is exactly what the reconciliation checks exist to catch. `secondary_copy_independent` (18), added 2026-11-05, is the same trick one bucket over — see the bullet on the no-mark rule below — and it entered the same list of files plus the arithmetic gate itself.
- **A key listed twice in the ledger's totals-seed array silently doubles a global figure.** Adding `non_english_independent` on 2026-11-03 produced a global of 90 against a per-article sum of 45 because one edit had flattened two entries onto one line. Nothing failed — the seed is a list, not a set. When adding a tally figure, compare the written global against the sum of the dated CSV's rows before quoting either.
- `isHighlighted()` already refused a language-flagged row, so this rule changes **no exhibit mark** and needs no re-print; `tools/audit-highlights.js` confirms it. Expect it to move labels and bucket membership only. If a future change of this kind does move a mark, that is a separate defect.
- A change to a counting rule does not reach exhibits already captured, because each report's `status`, `confirm_state` and language flag were written once at capture time. Applying one is an offline sequence: the re-apply tool for the rule that changed (`tools/reapply-language.js --write`, or `tools/reapply-corroboration.js --write`), then `tools/reprint-exhibits.js --changed --write`, then `tools/audit-highlights.js` while nothing downstream has moved yet, then `tools/build-catalog.js --write` and **only then** `tools/build-ledger.js`, then `tools/build-review-sheet.js --md` and `tools/build-dashboard-data.js`, and finally `tools/test-pdf-fit.js`. Both re-apply tools are dry-run by default, back up what they touch, and print the mark flips; a row a person decided (`confirm_state = 'user-decided'`) is never changed by a re-apply; the re-printer refuses to save unless its applied mark count matches the rule. The order is not cosmetic — the audit needs the re-printed HTML but not the store, so it fails fast, and the ledger reads its rows out of the store, so rebuilding it against a stale store raises a defect and writes nothing.- **Checking the yellow highlights.** The marks are baked into each saved exhibit HTML and printed into its PDF, so nothing downstream notices when they stop matching the rule — the ledger reads the report JSON and the PDF is only a picture. `tools/audit-highlights.js` is the check: it replays the current rule over every filed page offline (headless browser, every network request aborted, no Scholar contact), and also verifies each exhibit PDF exists and is non-empty and that no row which does not stand for its work is marked (a language edition, a same-work fold or a patent-family copy). It exits 1 on any disagreement. Takes about 40 seconds for all 168 pages. It reads the saved HTML, not the PDF; the PDF check below is the one that reads the printed file.
- **Checking the PDFs themselves.** `tools/audit-pdf-highlights.js` reads each filed exhibit PDF with pdf.js (the pinned `pdfjs-dist` in `tools/package.json`; read-only, no network) and checks the highlights as printed. It collects every filled rectangle in `rgb(255, 242, 0)`, joins the lines of a wrapped title into one mark, then checks each row of the page in document order: a row the rule marks must have a mark over its title, a row it does not mark must have none, and a mark over no title fails. A PDF that is not one page fails. Run it with `--pub=<base>` for one publication or `--verbose` for every page. Expected on the current set: 168 pages, 1056 marks printed, equal to the rule's 1056. Four matching rules it depends on: (a) Scholar's link-type markers (`[HTML]`, `[PDF]`) are stripped with `tools/scholar-marker.js`, because the highlight covers only the title text; (b) text is read in PDF content order and matched with 5 pt slack, because subscripts (`AB5`, `B(C6F5)3`) sit below the baseline and sorting by position moves them; (c) a title that Scholar also quotes in a snippet is paired with its row by the whole text item. Where a title still repeats so it cannot be paired by position, its rows are checked by count (the copies under a mark must equal the rule-marked rows) and listed as notes, not as row-by-row results — the cid-based HTML audit remains the row-level check for those; (d) the audit reads the PDF's drawing operators, so a fill colour other than the highlight colour is never counted. Its negative test: the superseded pre-fix PDF of GLAD p1 still carries the old `cit-000511` mark and fails on that row. Run it after every re-print, together with `audit-highlights.js`, before filing.
- **Checking the PDFs against their HTML.** `tools/audit-pdf-against-html.js` compares, row by row, the marks printed in each exhibit PDF with the marks in its saved HTML — the file the PDF was printed from. The two audits above each check one side against the counting rule; this one checks that the artefacts agree with each other, so a PDF that drifted from its HTML cannot pass both. HTML rows are paired by `data-cid` (`tools/row-match.js`, the same join as the re-printer); PDF marks are matched to the title they cover. It fails on any row whose mark differs between the two, on any mark count that differs, and on a repeated title whose copies disagree with the HTML. Run with `--pub=<base>` or `--verbose`. Expected on the current set: 168 pages compared, 1056 marks in each. Its negative test: the superseded pre-fix GLAD p1 PDF against the current HTML differs on the `cit-000511` row (HTML unmarked, PDF marked).
- **Compare highlight sets row by row, never by count.** A page where one row gains a mark and another loses one keeps its total, so any `before === want` filter passes it. Found 2026-11-05: `reprint-exhibits.js --changed` skipped `glad-glycan-…-p6` ("marks 9 -> 9") for two days while the exhibit carried two wrong marks. The tell is an audit line reading **"marks 4 (want 4)" with a per-row swap listed under it** — the counts agree and the rows do not. Both the audit and the re-printer now compare per row; do not reintroduce a count comparison in either.
- **A row is matched by Scholar's `data-cid`, never by its title.** Row-by-row comparison is only as good as the join, and three exhibit pages print the same title twice (Factor XI antibodies; CD137/cIAPs; Stabilizing camptothecin) — so a title join gives both rows the *first* matching entry's answer. That is what made the re-printer report those pages "already correct" on 2026-11-05 when one of the two copies had to lose its mark: the rule was right and the join was blind. Scholar stamps a `data-cid` on each `.gs_r.gs_or` row; it is unique per row and 1:1 with the report's `cid` on all 168 filed pages, so it is the join. The shared matcher is **`tools/row-match.js`**, used by both `reprint-exhibits.js` and `audit-highlights.js` — do not reimplement the pairing in a caller. It reports a basis per row (`cid` / `title` / `no-entry` / `ambiguous`); a repeated title with no cid is `ambiguous`, `want` echoes the current mark, and **the page is not saved** rather than guessed at. Both tools additionally hard-fail when the page's expected mark count disagrees with the count derived from the entries.
- **A check that asks a hypothetical proves nothing.** The audit's third check asked whether a folded copy *would* be marked *if it stood* (`isHighlightCandidate`, which ignores the duplicate decision by design) rather than whether the page carried a mark. It flagged exhibits that were exactly right and could not have detected a copy that actually was marked. When adding a check, ask what it can fail on: if no file state can make it fire, it is not a check.
- **Per the user's decision on 2026-11-05, an exhibit marks only the rows that stand for their work.** A row Scholar lists twice against the *same* cited paper — a journal record with its preprint, repository copy, thesis or patent-family twin — prints **plain**, as does a language edition. The dashboard keeps its own colour for that bucket; the PDF does not mark it. So `isHighlighted()` in `tools/tally.js` refuses a row for which `doesNotStand(e)` is true, and the number of yellow marks (1,078) equals the number of counted independent citations (1,078) — the old 1,094-vs-1,077 gap is gone and must not be reintroduced. Two things make this rule subtle. **(a) An absent standing flag means "no decision", not "does not stand".** `doesNotStand` reads `is_secondary_copy` (report shape) or `is_primary_copy` (store shape) and returns false when neither is present, because 0 of 171 filed report files carry either field — treating `undefined` as a copy blanks every exhibit. **(b) Do not recompute standing-ness inside the mark rule.** It needs the whole citing list, and `uniquePapers` → `copyReliability` → `isHighlighted` is circular; the tie-break in `copyReliability` and the cross-page "printed" test in `markLanguageEditions` therefore read `isHighlightCandidate` instead (measured: 0 flips of any standing copy, 0 divergence between the store and report paths over 3 cross-page edition groups).
- **An unmarked copy is not unsettled work.** A row that is INDEPENDENT, English, settled, and unmarked only because it does not stand is named by `tally.isSecondaryIndependent` and published as `secondary_copy_independent` (18) — it is *not* folded into `independent_pending`, which is open author work and reads 0 since the queue closed. Without the named term the rule change would have silently moved pending 0 → 17 and drawn an "Independent, unsettled" bucket on the waffle, telling a reviewer 17 questions were open when none is. Same reasoning as the 2026-11-03 language collapse: if no reading of the row can change the packet, do not call it pending. `isSettled` is required by the predicate so a genuinely unsettled second copy stays in `independent_pending`. The dashboard's `pendingRows` guard in `build-dashboard-data.js` mirrors the predicate — when it fails, narrow the query to match the rule, never relax the guard.
- **Three bases, and only one of them is a paper count.** The record is measured three ways and the names of two of the ledger columns invite confusing them:
  - `citation_records_reviewed` = **1,498** rows printed on the filed exhibit pages.
  - `independent_countable` = **1,078** rows carrying a yellow mark — and since 2026-11-05 that is also the counted figure, so the two agree by construction. Before that decision it read **1,094**, 17 more than the counted basis, because both listings of a duplicated paper were marked.
  - `independent_unique_papers` / `bucket_independent` = **1,078** *counted independent citations* — the packet's headline. Despite the name this is **per citation, not per paper**: `applyPrimaryCopy` in `tools/build-catalog.js` partitions by `cites_id`, so a work cited by two of the PI's publications keeps one standing row under each and contributes two.
  - **918** distinct independent citing papers, and **1,153** distinct citing papers overall. These are the only true paper counts; `build-dashboard-data.js` publishes them as `distinct_independent_papers` / `distinct_citing_papers` (plus `_english` variants), derived from `COALESCE(NULLIF(same_work_key,''), work_key)`.
  Expect **1,078** both when reconciling PDFs to the ledger and when quoting the packet (it was 1,077 until the Factor XI correction below, same day). The **160** between 1,078 and 918 are genuine double-citing, which the counted basis deliberately **keeps** — a paper citing two of the PI's works is two citations and is marked once on each of two exhibit pages. Do not describe that gap with the same word used for a duplicate listing.
- **`tools/test-catalog-merge.js` WRITES TO THE REAL STORE.** It calls `runBuilder(["--write"])` twice against `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite`, not a copy, so running it silently mutates the durable store (it did on 2026-11-05, moving the store 1094 → 1077 with a fresh `pre-merge` backup and no `--write` anywhere in the command). Run it deliberately, and rebuild the ledger afterwards if a figure matters. Prefer a scratch copy for anything exploratory.
- **Never label a figure "distinct papers" unless its numerator is one.** The `unique_*` column names predate this note and count citations, so a bar labelled "distinct papers" reading 1,078 against a real paper count of 918 is a discrepancy a reviewer should never be left to reconcile. When adding a listing, name the basis in the label — "counted citations" vs "distinct papers" — and route any new "papers" claim through one of the four `distinct_*` fields.
- Run the audit **after every batch of decisions or rule changes, not once at the end**. A drift found in the batch that caused it names the rows involved; a drift found after a hundred more decisions has to be bisected. `tools/apply-decision.js --rebuild` runs it inside the chain, immediately after the re-print and **before** the store is rebuilt, so a disagreement stops the chain with the ledger, review sheet and dashboard all still showing the last consistent state — a packet whose figures moved while its exhibits did not is the failure worth paying an extra step to avoid. A normal decision batch is therefore already audited; do not treat a separate audit run as optional busywork after anything that bypassed that tool.
- Run `tools/audit-everything.js` before any filing or hand-off. It runs every read-only check in one pass (unit tests, store against reports, ledger and dashboard arithmetic and freshness, the corroboration re-apply status, the HTML and PDF highlight audits, PDF against HTML, the one-sheet fit test, and a cross-source figure check: store, ledger and PDF marks must agree). `--quick` skips the browser-based checks. It fails on any FAIL and reports WARN lines without failing, so a pending decision such as the un-applied corroboration changes is visible rather than hidden. It deliberately never runs a writer: `build-ledger.js`, `build-catalog.js --write`, `build-dashboard-data.js`, `reprint-exhibits.js` and `test-catalog-merge.js` (which writes to the real store) are excluded.
- Never conclude highlights are correct by looking at a PDF, and never "fix" a highlighted row by editing the exhibit HTML or PDF. The re-printer is the only thing that redraws an exhibit, from the rules; if the audit disagrees, the report data or the rule is wrong.
- `tools/test-pdf-fit.js` measures **the most recently modified** saved citing HTML unless a page is passed explicitly, so a pass or failure says nothing about the other pages. Pass a page, or pass `--all`. Since the 0.73 scale change on 2026-11-02 every one of the 168 filed citing exhibits prints to one sheet; the two profile exhibits (`akul-mehta-google-scholar-*.pdf`, 48 rows) are expected to run long. `tools/audit-highlights.js` now also fails on any citing exhibit PDF that prints to more than one sheet, so a future rule or content change that tips a page over is caught rather than discovered at filing.
- Per the user's rule on 2026-11-02, a preprint or `[CITATION]` entry is recorded as a duplicate of a journal record **only when it is demonstrably the same work**. A preprint server alone is not the test, and neither is a similar title. Where the titles differ, deeper evidence is required before merging — a matching complete byline plus matching venue/DOI chain, or the published paper's own statement of a prior version. Without that, the row is classified on its own merits: if its author list shares nobody with the cited work and names neither PI, it is **independent**, because it appears independent. Merging on suspicion both hides a real citation and rests on an unproven identity claim in a filing. Once a same-work copy is recorded, the dashboard labels it "Preprint of the published article" when it sits on a preprint server (2026-11-07). A same-work copy inherits its parent's verdict, and that parent may be settled by an external record (`external-resolved`) as well as by Scholar's list or a person (2026-11-07; cit-001247 is the case).
- The converse also holds: `tools/tally.js` `paperKey` merges rows on a normalised identical title only, so a differently-titled preprint is never auto-merged and needs the manual evidence above. When two rows are left as separate works, the distinct-paper figure counts them as two — say so plainly rather than implying the packet proves they are one paper.
- Where the evidence **does** meet that bar, record the identity with `tools/apply-decision.js --row=<uid> --same-work-as=<anchor uid> --note="..."` (the note is required — an unproven identity claim in a filing is exactly what the rule above prevents). It writes `same_work_key` on the rows and nothing else: status, confirm_state, title and the exhibit mark are untouched. `tally.foldSameWork` is the single place a fold becomes a consequence — it picks the copy that stands, points the rest at it via `duplicate_of`, and sets `duplicate_kind = 'same-work'` so a same-work fold is never blurred with a language edition. Both `groupReports` and `build-catalog.applyEditions` call it; do not reimplement it. `uniquePapers` groups on `same_work_key` when present, which is what stops a preprint and its published article counting as two papers. `--revert` takes the fold off again.
- **A title-keyed fold is a guess and can be wrong; a recorded `same_work_key` is how to undo one.** `paperKey` groups on a normalised title alone, so two genuinely different works that Scholar happens to title identically collapse into one — which silently un-marks the second under the 2026-11-05 no-mark-on-copies rule. Found and corrected the same day on `t:factorxiantibodiesandmethodsofuse`: `cit-000027` (US20170022292A1, inventors Eder et al., priority 2015-06-26 from provisionals 62/184,955 and 62/341,568) was standing for the group while `cit-000030` (US11168147B2) and `cit-000032` (US12012464B2), both Aigner/Koch/Waldhuber with priority 2016-12-23, were folded away. US12012464B2 states on its face that it is a continuation of Ser. No. 16/472,646, which issued as US11168147B2, so 030 and 032 are one work and 027 is a separate family. **No new tool was needed to unfold it**: `uniquePapers` groups on `same_work_key` when a person recorded one and only otherwise falls back to the title, so `--row=cit-000032 --same-work-as=cit-000030` lifts that pair out of the title bucket and 027 falls back to the title key and stands again — the unfold falls out of a fold. Expect `distinct_independent_papers` to rise by exactly **one**, not two, because the anchor takes the new key while the remainder keeps the title key.
- **Never push a verdict through on a row that is not the copy standing for its work.** `apply-decision.js` refuses it and says the highlight would move off the standing copy; that refusal is the tool protecting an exhibit, not an obstacle. If one was written by mistake, `--revert --write` restores the exact prior state — do not reach for `--allow-mark-move` to get past the warning. Related trap: Scholar can render the same person's name in **inverted forms** across two copies of one work (`AM Abdel` on the repository copy, `MHA Aziz` on the ProQuest copy of the same VCU dissertation), and surname-plus-initials matching cannot see they are one person — so one copy reads INDEPENDENT while its twin reads DEPENDENT against a paper naming that author. Recording the identity of such a work needs a fold **per cited paper** (which `foldProblem` enforces), and a fold is not a substitute for the classification: check what the standing copy against each cited paper actually says before deciding one.
- When two rows are copies of one paper, `copyReliability` in `tools/tally.js` picks which copy the decision is taken from. A **demonstrated** overlap with the cited work outranks a clean but blind read: a copy whose author list names the PI or the former PI decides the row even when the other copy has the more complete byline, because "this person is on both papers" is evidence and "I read a complete list that happened to be silent" is not. Found on 2026-11-02 with the VCU dissertation whose author shared no name with the paper but whose advisor was the former PI — the DEPENDENT copy had been losing to an INDEPENDENT one and a self-citation was being counted.
- **A fold must stay within one cited paper.** `foldSameWork` groups on `same_work_key` alone and never compares `cites_id`, then marks the losing copies `duplicate_of` — which `isHighlighted()` refuses. So a fold that crossed cited papers would silently remove a highlight from one exhibit. The mistake is easy to make because one citing article appears on the "cited by" page of *every* paper it cites: two rows can be the same WORK while being two separate CITATIONS, and independence is relative to the cited paper. Measured 2026-11-03, **178 title-keyed groups span more than one cited paper**, so the confusion is common in this corpus. `foldProblem()` in `tools/apply-decision.js` is the gate and refuses the whole batch; it also refuses when either side has no `cites_id`, because "unknown" must never be read as "same". The 178 are correct as they stand — one distinct work, genuinely that many citations — and must never be folded.
- Adding a signal to `copyReliability`, `uniquePapers` or any tally figure means adding its inputs to **every** projection out of the store: `applyPrimaryCopy` in `tools/build-catalog.js` and `storeEntries()` in `tools/build-ledger.js`. Both compute the same numbers from copied rows, so a field left out of one makes the two disagree and the reconciliation gate fails — which is the guard working, not a bug to route around.
- Preserve the user's existing files and organization. Make narrowly scoped changes and do not silently discard or overwrite user-authored material.
- Exhibit PDFs must look like a Google Scholar results page where only counted independent citations are highlighted in yellow, and only on the row that stands for the work (2026-11-05). Do not add legends, review marks, or faded rows to an exhibit; keep such annotations in the separate review notes or behind a debug flag. The dashboard may use a distinct colour for the preprint/copy bucket — the PDF may not.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-10-29, every exhibit PDF page must print a header showing the Google Scholar URL it was captured from (plus the snapshot date) and a footer with page numbers. This is the one permitted annotation; it overrides the earlier no-print-header rule.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02, exhibit PDFs print on US Letter at **73%** scale. The original 75% (2026-10-29) left three tall citing pages printing to two sheets; the user asked for a slight reduction, and 0.73 is the highest scale measured to put every filed citing page on one sheet (0.74 still overflows). The scale, margins and format live in one module, `tools/print-settings.js`, imported by the capture, the re-printer, the profile capture and the fit test — never restate them inline, since five copies drifting apart is what let the exhibits disagree silently.
- `tools/test-pdf-fit.js` decides by counting the sheets the printed PDF actually has, not by measuring where the last result row ends. The old row-bottom arithmetic reported all 170 pages fitting while three filed exhibits were genuinely two sheets, because snippets and links below the last row's own box still print. `--all` checks every saved citing page (a few workpapers wider than the filed set) and exits 1 on any multi-sheet page. Note it still reports the most recently modified saved page unless one is passed explicitly, so a single-page pass says nothing about the others.
- Google Scholar shows 10 citing articles per page for this profile, and a `pagesize=20` parameter does not change that. Page through a citing list by following the page's own "Next" link, which carries Scholar's real step size and query parameters; hand-built `start=` offsets drop parameters such as `as_sdt`, `sciodt`, and `scipsc` and silently skip records. Expect roughly one page per 10 citations.
- Greek letters in a title are scientific notation, not evidence of a non-English paper (for example an alpha-1,2-mannosidase or beta-catenin title is English). Treat a small number of Greek letters alongside substantial Latin text as notation and do not suppress the citation; only flag it when Greek letters make up the body of the text. Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-02 this is implemented as a **share** test, not a count: `tools/capture-citations.js` flags Greek only above 25% of the letters, and a stray non-Latin character in a snippet flags only above the same share (one Cyrillic epsilon in a chemical-name abstract is a rendering artifact, not a foreign-language entry).
- A byline year is Scholar's rendering of a venue, not a verified publication date, and it is sometimes the date of a parent reference work. `cit-000036` ("Anticoagulants", DOI `10.1002/0471266949.bmc182.pub2`, a *Burger's Medicinal Chemistry* chapter Crossref-dated 2021-04-26) carries **2003** because Scholar itself prints 2003 — confirmed against the filed exhibit HTML, so it is not a capture artifact. The year chart in `tools/build-dashboard-data.js` therefore refuses a parsed date earlier than the year of the paper cited, since a citing work cannot predate its source, and publishes each exclusion in `year_anomalies` so the caption names the rows rather than letting a year vanish silently. Only a known `cited_year` may exclude a row; an empty one is unknown, not evidence.
- **Do not delete a counted citation to tidy a chart.** Removing `cit-000036` would move independent 1078 → 1077 and require exhibit page 4 to be re-printed, which is a filing decision for the user through `tools/apply-decision.js`, not a dashboard cleanup. Fixing a derived chart and changing filed evidence are different acts; when a date is wrong but the citation is real, exclude the date and say so.
- Every chart that splits a publication's records must use the same exhaustive bucket set as the waffle, with `review_queue` rather than raw `review` and the non-English rows in their own bucket, so a bar's segments add up to its record count. A stack drawn at zero still emits a legend key, which reads as hidden work — draw `independent_pending` only when some row actually has it.
- Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-03, **every listing of citing works leads with `row_uid`**, the same `span.uid` column the review queue, unsettled and non-English tables use — including the per-work list on `works.html` and the citing-patents table on `index.html`. A row must be nameable by its permanent uid from anywhere, since a title plus exhibit page is not a stable handle. The table's search box must match on the uid too.
- **A `@media print` rule only takes effect on the shared browser page, not a freshly created one.** Setting `Emulation.setEmulatedMedia` over CDP on a `newPage()` leaves `matchMedia('print').matches` false, so a check reports `table-layout: auto` and a phantom overflow and looks like broken CSS. Emulate on the already-open page, and set the emulation *after* navigation.
- **Measure table width against the sheet whenever a column is added.** Chrome clips whatever hangs past the page edge and warns about nothing: `#patents-table` was 869px against 663px available and had been losing its last printed column silently until the uid column made it obvious. `table-layout: fixed` with weighted `th` widths in the print block is the fix already used for the other appendix tables.
- **A dashboard chapter number is written in four places.** `PAGES` in `dashboard/js/core.js` drives the contents bar, and the same number is also hardcoded in each page's `<p class="chapter-num">`, its kicker line, its header comment, and the numbered list on `index.html`. Nothing at runtime reconciles them, so inserting a page silently leaves every later page labelled with its old number — which happened on 2026-11-05 when `partition.html` went in after overview, and the bar said "4. Per publication" while the page said "chapter 3". `tools/check-dashboard-nav.js` is the check: read-only, exits 1 naming the exact page and which of the four sites disagrees, and it fails loudly if the `PAGES` array or the contents-list markup ever changes shape so the check would go blind. Run it after touching any page's number.

## Notable-Citations Packet Is Separate From the Record

- **Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-06, the notable-citations / lawyer-packet effort is separate from the Independent Citation Record: read from the record freely, write to it not at all.** The record is `Independent Citation Record/` (guide, `Exhibits/`, `Progress Tracker.json`), `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite`, and the `dashboard/` fed from it; it has its own audit chain and a reconciliation gate, and the packet is only a presentation built on top. Write packet output inside `Citations/Notable Citations Packet/`. This means **no logging packet work in `Progress Tracker.json`** — a progress line is a write, and I did exactly that on 2026-11-06 before the rule was given and reverted it (`git checkout` of that one file; the record was back to its committed 66 log entries). Keep packet status in `Citations/Notable Citations Packet/PACKET-STATUS.md`.
- **The trap is that the shared `tools/` mostly write.** `apply-decision.js`, `build-catalog.js --write`, `build-ledger.js`, `reprint-exhibits.js --write`, `reapply-language.js`, `reapply-corroboration.js`, `refetch-corroboration.js`, `build-dashboard-data.js`, `build-review-sheet.js` and the capture scripts all mutate the record, and `tools/test-catalog-merge.js` writes the real store **even with no `--write` flag**. Read-only and safe: `query-catalog.js`, `tally.js`, the dated ledger CSV, the exhibit PDFs, and `parse-citation-summary.js` (opens the store `readOnly: true`, writes only `Citations/Citation-summary.md`). Install any new dependency (e.g. `pdfjs-dist`) under the packet folder, not `tools/package.json`, so the record's toolchain is untouched.
- **If the packet surfaces a defect in the record, report it — do not fix it from this side.** A correction applied here bypasses the audit sequence and leaves filed exhibits disagreeing with the packet's figures.
- **Per the user's question on 2026-11-06, the packet keeps its *own* SQLite database** — `Citations/Notable Citations Packet/notable-citations.sqlite`, tables `citation` and `file` — and the CSVs are derived reports of it. It must **not** go into `Database/citation-catalog.sqlite`: that file is the record's durable store, `tools/build-catalog.js` merges into it and treats it as the record's projection of the per-page reports, and packet commentary (tier judgements, screening opinions, prose for counsel) must never be recoverable as though it were filed evidence. The separate file is also what makes the boundary physical rather than a rule to remember: it can be zipped to counsel or deleted without touching the record. Read the record `readOnly: true`; no cross-file foreign keys (SQLite cannot enforce them anyway) — validate `row_uid`s by query.
- **Keep the screened-out records.** Per the user on 2026-11-06, every candidate considered gets a row with `status` (`included` / `screened-out` / `held`) and `screen_reason`; deleting one destroys the only record of why the packet is the size it is and guarantees the same article gets reconsidered from scratch. Export `packet.csv` (included) and `screened-out.csv` (the rest) from the same table so the counts cannot disagree, and show the exclusions to counsel as a factual appendix. `held` means open work and must also appear in `PACKET-STATUS.md`.
- **Packet PDF names carry the citing senior author** — `papers/cit-000544/03-article-Heras-2024.pdf` — because counsel browses the folder in Explorer, where a bare uid says nothing. Use the last author of the published article, ASCII-folded (`Guerardel`), no initials. The name is a label, not an identifier: `folder_uid` and `source_pdf` remain the join, and surnames collide.
- **A paywalled article is fetched through the Playwright MCP Chrome, not `fetch-browser-pdf.js`.** The user's proxy and institutional login live in the MCP browser's profile (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\ms-playwright-mcp\…`); `tools/human.js` launches `tools/.playwright-profile`, which has no grant, so the script's window shows a wall on a page the user can read. The MCP server has **no filesystem access from page code** — `require`, `import`, and `process` are all unavailable inside `browser_run_code_unsafe`, and that tool's `filename` parameter *reads* code from a file rather than writing a result. The route that works, verified 2026-11-08 on `cit-000595` (OUP *Glycobiology*): `browser_navigate` to the article, let Cloudflare's interstitial clear on its own (`browser_wait_for` with `textGone`, never interact with the check), then in `browser_run_code_unsafe` do `page.request.get(pdfUrl, { headers: { Referer: articleUrl } })` and return `buf.toString('base64')`. The harness offloads the large result to a temp file; decode it with a local `.cjs` that matches `/"b64"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"/`, checks the `%PDF-` magic, and writes the bytes. Then follow the normal filing chain.
- **ScienceDirect's PDF is earned by navigation, not by a request.** `/science/article/pii/<PII>/pdf` answers `page.request.get` with 403, but `page.goto` redirects to a **single-use** signed `pdf.sciencedirectassets.com/...main.pdf?X-Amz-…` URL that the browser viewer consumes. Re-requesting that URL (even with the same cookies) returns an HTML error page, and `goto`'s own `response.body()` fails with `No resource with given identifier found` once the navigation commits. The working recipe: attach `page.on('response', …)` **before** `goto`, call `r.body()` inside the handler on the first response whose `content-type` contains `pdf`, and poll for the captured buffer. Verified 2026-11-08 on 7 rows.
- **ACS serves a 601-byte HTML viewer stub labelled `content-type: application/pdf`, so response-body capture cannot see the file — `route.fetch()` can.** On `pubs.acs.org`, both `page.request.get` on `/doi/pdf/` and on `/…/article-pdf/…` return 403 (fingerprint-blocked API context), and the navigation response that reports itself as a PDF is a 601-byte `<iframe>` placeholder; the real bytes go into the Chrome PDF extension (`chrome-extension://mhjfbmdgcfjbbpaeojofohoefgiehjai/…`) and never appear as a capturable response. The working recipe, verified 2026-11-08 on 6 rows: warm the grant by `goto`-ing the **article** page and waiting out "Just a moment…", then `page.route('**/doi/pdf/**', …)` with a handler doing `route.fetch({ headers: { Accept: 'application/pdf', Referer: articleUrl } })` → `resp.body()` → `route.fulfill()`. That returns the genuine `%PDF-` bytes (4.9 MB on `cit-000010`). Two traps: reloading the PDF URL instead of re-warming the article page re-triggers Cloudflare, and the magic check must compare **4** bytes against `'%PDF'` — comparing 5 against `'%PDF'` silently discards every capture.
- **Navigating to the PDF viewer wipes `window`, so a batch stash does not survive it.** Stashing each capture on `window.__pdfs` and looping works on Wiley (where `page.request.get` never leaves the page), but on ScienceDirect the `goto` clears the stash between articles. Either dump one article per cycle (`goto 'about:blank'` → stash → `browser_evaluate(..., {filename})`), or stash on a **separate** `about:blank` page obtained from `page.context().pages()`. Don't assume a helper page is available: `ctx.newPage()` then `p.close()` closed the whole context once here — never close a page you did not create, and never `browser_close`.
- **Check a stored `pdf_url`'s extension before trusting it.** `cit-000941`'s queue URL was `ars.els-cdn.com/content/image/…-ga1_lrg.jpg` — a graphical abstract, not the article. Rebuild the request from the DOI's PII instead of downloading whatever URL the crawler recorded.
- **"Harvard University does not subscribe to this content on ScienceDirect" is a finding, not a wall.** When the OpenAthens session renders that sentence on the abstract page, no route exists and retrying wastes the session — mark the row `no-open-copy` with the sentence quoted (as on `cit-000147`, *Journal of Functional Foods*). Distinguish it from a Cloudflare challenge, which the user can clear.
- **An Elsevier "Journal Pre-proof" PDF is the accepted manuscript, not the typeset version of record** — page 1 of `cit-000775` says so. It is still the cited content, but record the fact in the tracker note so the classification pass can decide whether to file it.
- **`page.request.get` succeeds where in-page `fetch` and browser navigation both fail.** On OUP, `browser_evaluate` + `fetch` throws `TypeError: Failed to fetch` and navigating to the `/article-pdf/` URL 302s to a `watermark02.silverchair.com` signed URL that dies with `net::ERR_FAILED`. The API request context is not subject to the page's CSP and does not get the watermark redirect. Ask for the `content-type` and refuse anything that is not `application/pdf` — a 200 returning an HTML login page is the failure mode to catch.
- **Harvard's proxy is OpenAthens, not EZproxy** (user correction, 2026-11-08). The `*.ezp-prod1.hul.harvard.edu` host-rewrite prints a "EZproxy Service Retirement" page. The live route is the user's bookmarklet form: navigate `https://go.openathens.net/redirector/library.harvard.edu?url=<encoded article URL>`, which SAML-redirects to HarvardKey sign-in; the user signs in once and the grant lives in the MCP profile afterwards. Wrapping the **PDF** URL works too, but wrapping the article URL and then requesting the PDF is enough.
- **Wiley's `/doi/pdf/<doi>` is an HTML reader shell, not the file.** Navigating it leaves the tab on an HTML page whose embedded viewer fetches `https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/<doi>` — that endpoint is what answers `application/pdf`, and only once entitled (without entitlement it 302s back to `/doi/abs/`, and the in-page "Download PDF" click gives 403). When a publisher hides the real asset behind a viewer, watch the traffic: `page.on('response', …)` filtered on `content-type: pdf` names the URL to request. Verified 2026-11-08 across 15 rows on `cit-000008`.
- **One publisher grant covers the publisher's whole batch — request the other hosts' rows through it too.** After the Wiley sign-in, `pdfdirect` served three rows whose stored `pdf_url` pointed somewhere else and 403'd: `cit-000935` (PMC), `cit-001019` (Hindawi, journal since moved to Wiley), `cit-001305` (jthjournal.org). So when a row's own link is walled but the article has a DOI on a host you are entitled to, try that host before marking the row `walled`.
- **Stash a batch on `window.__pdfs` and write one JSON dump, not one dump per article.** `page.evaluate(() => { window.__pdfs[uid] = b64 })` between fetches, then a single `browser_evaluate(() => JSON.stringify(window.__pdfs), {filename: '…'})`. `page.request.get` bodies live in the Playwright process, so the base64 has to cross into the page via `evaluate` — and `window` does **not** exist inside `browser_run_code_unsafe` itself, only inside the callback passed to `page.evaluate`. Decode with a `.cjs` that unwraps repeatedly while `typeof JSON.parse(text) === 'string'`, because `browser_evaluate` writes its result JSON-encoded (a string payload arrives double-encoded).
- **Downloaded PDFs land in `Notable Citations Packet/downloads/<row_uid>.pdf` first**, which is the inbox `fetch-browser-pdf.js` already uses. Do not invent a new folder: `file-pdf.js --src=` takes a path under `Citations/` and copies it into the status-correct root itself (`papers/`, `pending-papers/`, or `screened-papers/`), and it runs a title check against the extracted text before writing — that check is what proves a paywall PDF is the right article and not a cookie-wall landing page.
- **Never close the MCP browser or its first tab.** (User instruction, 2026-11-08, superseding the earlier "close each tab after its PDF is on disk".) `browser_close` quits the whole browser, which destroys every Cloudflare and institutional-access grant the user earned by hand — the loss costs more than a tidy tab list. Reuse one working tab for the whole session, and treat the user's own tabs as off-limits; they said they would keep one tab open for themselves. This replaces the per-article close habit, which was based on tidiness and turned out to be destructive.
- **For a large PDF, write the base64 to a file instead of returning it.** A 6.4 MB ChemRxiv PDF is 8.5 MB of base64, which exceeds the tool-result limit and gets offloaded to an unreadable temp file. `browser_evaluate`'s `filename` parameter *does* write its result, so stash the string on `window` in `browser_run_code_unsafe` and read it out with `browser_evaluate(() => window.__pdfB64, {filename: '…'})`. Two cautions: the path resolves against the **repo root**, so delete the dump afterwards rather than committing 8 MB of text, and never use this to write cookies — that is how `oup-cookies.txt` once appeared at the repo root.
- **A Cloudflare grant can be per-path, not per-origin.** On ChemRxiv (`cit-000640`) the article page loaded fine while `page.request.get` on the `/doi/pdf/` URL returned 403. `browser_navigate` to the PDF URL itself, have the user clear the wall on *that* URL, and the same `page.request.get` then returns 200 `application/pdf` — the clearance the browser earned on the article did not carry to the PDF endpoint. Same on OUP (`cit-000914`): the article page cleared on its own, the `/article-pdf/` path did not.
- **PMC's PDF endpoint has its own interstitial, and it self-clears.** `/articles/PMC…/pdf/<id>.pdf` answers 200 with an HTML "Preparing to download …" page to `page.request.get`, and `browser_navigate` lands on "Checking your browser - reCAPTCHA". Leave the tab alone (never click the check) and after roughly a minute the same `page.request.get` returns 200 `application/pdf` — verified 2026-11-08 on `cit-000923` (8.8 MB). Re-test with `page.request` rather than reading the tab's title, which can change before the page reports anything.
- **A "no mention found" scan is only a finding if the extraction worked.** Before concluding a citing article does not use a tool, check the extracted text length and count a word you expect to be there (`microarray` 11 times on `cit-000923`). A failed reader returns empty text, which `scan-mentions.js` reports identically to an article that genuinely never names the tool.
- **A `null` `citing_senior_author` makes `file-pdf.js` name the file literally `01-article-article-<year>.pdf`.** The slug falls back to the word "article", which stops the filename saying who wrote the paper (§5.1). Record the name through `set-senior-author.js`'s `FIXES` table — read off page 1 of the retrieved article, with the basis in the note, never inferred from Scholar's truncated byline — then rename the file and update `file.file` and `citation.pdf_file` together. `validate-packet.js`'s `[pdf-name]` check is what catches the mismatch.
- **A citing paper that never names the tool is resolved by `scan-refs.js`, not `scan-mentions.js`.** The tool appears only as a bibliography entry, so the scanner reports "References p.N -> unresolved" and that is a *correct* result, not a failure. Run `scan-refs.js --folder=<uid> --mentions=<file>` to resolve the entry's number to its in-text marker (including an orphan superscript on its own line), read the recovered sentence, then `record-mentions.js --check` and `--write`. The row's `basis` becomes `reference-number resolution` and the review page shows a blue "resolved" pill rather than a scanned tier.
- **A `held` row keeps `citation.tier` NULL by design; the evidence lives in `mention`.** Only `included` rows carry a headline tier, because a tier on a citation is a claim counsel reads. Measured 2026-11-08, 98 of 129 rows with a resolved mention have a NULL headline tier and a populated `mention.tier`. Do not "fix" the NULL — promote the row, or leave it.
- **Per the user's instruction on 2026-11-08, retrieval is its own pass: get the PDFs now, classify and catalogue afterwards.** `node scripts/download-queue.js` is the tracker — it lists the `held`/`review` rows grouped by publisher host so one cleared grant covers a batch, `--host=<substr>` and `--list` narrow it, `--mark=<uid>=<status>` records an outcome, and `--export` writes `download-queue.csv`. Retrieval states (`downloaded`, `walled`, `no-open-copy`, `skipped-preprint`, `skipped-thesis`, `failed`) live in the `download_attempt` table and are **not** the same thing as `candidate.discover_state`, which keeps its older narrower meaning; a row with no attempt row and no file on disk is simply pending. Commit in batches while classification is deferred, since there is no per-article tier to commit.
- **Do not retrieve preprints — published articles only** (user instruction, 2026-11-08). This narrows the earlier rule that a preprint was judged on its contents: for *retrieval*, a link to bioRxiv/MedRxiv/ChemRxiv/arXiv/OSF is skipped outright, and the published DOI is what to fetch if one exists. `download-queue.js` makes the guess from the **URL only**, never from a title, and exports the `kind` column so a person can overrule any row. A preprint of an article that has since published is not lost — the published version is the better exhibit anyway.
- **`mention.basis` is a CHECK-constrained enum** — `extracted text`, `docx note`, `reference-number resolution`, `human reading`. Inventing a descriptive basis aborts the whole `record-mentions.js` write, and because it aborts mid-transaction it can leave earlier rows in the batch already committed: fix the spec and re-run rather than assuming nothing was written. A `note` key in the spec is silently dropped (the INSERT has no such column), so context has to go somewhere that is read.
- **One citing article can carry several `row_uid`s and needs one stored PDF, but only for the rows whose cited work is actually in it.** `pdfForRow()` falls back to a row's *own* folder, so sibling rows must have `pdf_file` pointed at the shared path or their quotes cannot be verified (`dedup-files.js` is the precedent). CarboGrove (`cit-000428`/`cit-000743`/`cit-000914`/`cit-001462`) showed the limit: the three rows whose cited works appear in the published reference list share the file, and the bioRxiv-preprint row keeps no pointer because pointing it there would assert an identity nobody proved.
- **A single page can hold two sections, so read the heading position, not the page number.** In CarboGrove the GlyMDB and GLAD sentences sit at p.2 lines 3–6 while the `Results` heading is line 33 of that same page; a tier-B "used in Results" claim written from the page number alone would have been false, and both sentences are literature statements (Introduction, tier C).
- **`candidate` is a snapshot taken at seed time; `citation` is the authority.** `candidate.screen_state` lags `citation.status`: measured 2026-11-08, 54 rows were screened-out in `citation` while their candidate row still read `held`, and 610 held rows read `unscreened`. `work-type-report.js` prints the snapshot column, so **anything that decides whether a row is open work must query `citation.status` through `lib.openPacket()`, never the log's column** — a filter on it skipped 5 genuinely held GLAD rows and would have re-offered the 54 decided ones. `validate-packet.js` still uses `candidate` to enumerate the queued works, which is fine for a work list and wrong for a per-row gate.
- **A bulk screen tool must skip rows a person already decided, and a re-sweep must confirm a screen rather than restate one.** `screen-from-report.js` used to treat every SECONDARY row as open work, so a GLAD re-sweep overwrote the concise human `screen_reason` on two already-screened rows with bulk evidence prose. The reasons were restored verbatim through `set-screen.js`. Diff the DB against `HEAD` after any bulk write (`git show HEAD:<path>` to a temp copy, then compare column by column) — that is what found it, and it is also how to prove a batch touched only the rows intended.
- **A rule change must be re-applied to work screened before the rule existed.** Adding the PubMed MeSH route (2026-11-08) meant the 733 held rows were still holding whatever the three older routes said. Re-sweeping all 34 works is ~9 min (`work-type-report.js` at roughly 1.6s/row) and found 3 rows that genuinely qualified. Run it per work and commit per work, so a screen is attributable to the publication it came from.
- **The `[potential]` check is row-level, on purpose.** It reproduces the screen (`lib.potentialIndependent` over every queued work) and fails if the page omits any row the screen offers. It used to require every queued *work* to appear on the page, which fired the moment a work's last held row was screened — a finished work is not a missing one (MAWE, `b9d5057`). Keep the 0-rows-offered branch too: an empty review page means the pipeline stopped, not that the reviewing finished.
- **`set-screen.js` refuses a batch containing an `included` row, so a plan that mixes statuses aborts wholesale.** That refusal is the tool protecting a filed exhibit. Build a plan from `citation.status = 'held'` before applying it rather than discovering the refusal mid-batch.

## Citing-Article PDFs (`Citations/`)

- `Citations/` holds the PDFs of articles that cite the PI's tools, filed by **where the citation appears**: `In Methods`, `In Acknowledgements`, `In Results and Figures`, `In high reputation Publication`, `low-value`, plus `Notable Citations in Original Application`. A file belongs at the top level only while nobody has read it.
- `Citations/Citation-summary.docx` is **hand-maintained by the user and is the source of truth**; never write to it. `tools/parse-citation-summary.js` renders it to `Citation-summary.md` — that file is generated, so edit the docx and re-run rather than editing the markdown. Run `--check` to report drift (it ignores the render-date line so it does not fire every morning).
- **The docx records *how* the user read each paper; the PDF now decides.** Google Scholar snippets are no help — a search of every active snippet for GLAD, GlycoGlyph, MAWE and `glycotoolkit` returned **0 rows** — but since 2026-11-06 the PDFs themselves are readable (see the extraction bullet below), so a docx claim can be checked against the article. Do that before filing, and report a disagreement rather than editing the docx: it is the user's source of truth and the generated markdown must keep reproducing exactly what they wrote. Word's formatting is the parse key — **title bold, authors plain, journal italic** — which is how a title is recovered for the catalog match without guessing at a comma.
- **Do not file a PDF as Methods evidence on the folder name or the tool name in the file name.** Read the row's note first. `Laura_Kiessling-MAWE-s41467-025-67099-4.pdf` was held unfiled on 2026-11-06 because the docx said the PDF text showed no in-text statement that MAWE was used and asked for reference 69 to be checked. On 2026-11-06 extraction settled it: ref 69 is the MAWE paper and the only **standalone** `69` — a bare superscript, which is why searching the text for the word "MAWE" finds only the reference list — sits at p15, after the Methods heading (p10) and before References (p17), inside "Assay of Itln2 on microbial and mammalian glycan array" — so it is filed under `In Methods`. (Two other `69` substrings on p13 are extinction coefficients, `ε = 69,830`, not citations.) **The caveat is part of the record: the citing sentence is hedged and observational** — *"in 2024, the core facility also changed protocols and began regenerating and reusing slides; the long-term effects on fluorescence intensity are unclear"* — it cites MAWE for slide regeneration, not "we performed MAWE". A file named for a tool is not by itself a citation *of* use of that tool.
- **PDF text *can* be read — the dependency-free route cannot.** There is no Python and no `pdftotext`, and a hand-rolled `zlib.inflateSync` of the content streams returns glyph indices from embedded subset fonts, which is what led an earlier session to conclude extraction was impossible. It is not: `npm install pdfjs-dist` then `pdfjs.getDocument({ data, useSystemFonts: true, isEvalSupported: false })` and group `getTextContent().items` by `it.transform[5]` (2.5-unit threshold, honour `hasEOL`) rebuilds readable lines. Verified 2026-11-06 on all 16 filed PDFs outside `Notable Citations in Original Application`. A `Required "glyf" table is not found` or `TT: undefined function` warning is cosmetic — those files still extracted every sentence. Do not conclude anything about a paper's contents from a *failed* extraction, but check whether it actually failed before blaming the PDF.
- **A tool mention is in Methods if a Methods heading precedes it and no later section heading intervenes — judge it from the heading, never from the sentence's page or the auto-label.** A classifier that stops at the first heading-like line is wrong twice over. A `Figure 3.` caption or a `2.5 | Lectin array in lysates` subsection hijacks everything after it, and the top-level heading it should have found is often not the plain word: van der Wal prints `2 | M E T H O D S` with letterspacing (the spaces defeat a `^Methods$` test and the row read "no enclosing section"), and `GlycoGlyph-LeGenD-2026.pdf` labels its Methods `Experimental procedures`. Allow letterspaced spellings and the synonyms `Experimental procedures` / `Experimental Section`, and ignore numbered subsections and figure captions. Measured 2026-11-06: `GLAD-Wilson-2026.pdf` reads "Results" in the docx because three figure captions use GLAD, but Methods on p10 also names it — so the folder is right and the docx label is merely narrower.
- **Every filed PDF was read and its folder confirmed on 2026-11-06; do not re-litigate a placement without new evidence.** Of the 21 PDFs outside `Notable Citations in Original Application`: **12 of the 14 `In Methods` files name a tool literally inside Methods** (which some journals call `Material and Methods`, singular, or `Experimental procedures`); `GLAD-heras-2023-original-bioarchive-preprint-webpage.pdf` is a printout of the bioRxiv landing page so it contains no tool mention at all and is row 1 supporting material, not an article; and `Laura_Kiessling-MAWE…pdf` marks Methods with a **bare superscript reference number**, which a text search for the word "MAWE" cannot see — only the reference list spells the tool out. `In Results and Figures` (Maares: Results + Discussion, never Methods), `In high reputation Publication` (Kinoshita: Introduction only, a review) and all three `low-value` files (one names MAWE in its reference list alone; two never mention a tool) each match their folder. Two placements look wrong and are not: `GLAD-Wilson-2026.pdf`, where Methods names GLAD although the docx note was written from the figure captions, and the bioRxiv webpage printout above.
- **One citing article can carry several `row_uid`s, so never treat a uid count as an article count.** Measured 2026-11-06 over the 14 `In Methods` files: five articles hold more than one row — Heras `cit-000544`/`cit-000558`, Hokke `cit-000518`/`cit-000551`, Georgiev/Jamieson `cit-000629`/`cit-001261`, and Gerardo Vasta and Guérardel with **4 rows each**. Group on the store's `paper_key`, then check the leftovers against the docx. Two different causes, and the distinction decides how many citations exist: several rows citing **several of the PI's papers** are several citations (Gerardo Vasta cites GLAD, GlycoGlyph, the glycobiology review and MAWE — one article, four citations), while rows citing the *same* PI paper are duplicate listings of one citation (Hokke, and Heras).
- **Heras is the case where `paper_key` does *not* group, and that is not a defect to fix silently.** Its two rows sit under different `paper_key`s because Scholar lists the bioRxiv preprint and the journal article under different titles, so the store refuses to assert they are one work — which is the correct behaviour of a rule that groups on a normalised title alone. What says they are one article is `Citation-summary.docx` entry 1 (same authors under both titles, preprint 29 Apr 2023 → article accepted 8 Jul 2024, straddling the 25 Apr 2024 filing). Present it as one citing work with three PDFs and say the identity rests on the documents, not the database; folding it in the record is the user's call via `tools/apply-decision.js --same-work-as`, and the ledger keeps counting both highlighted rows either way because its basis is counted citations, not distinct articles.
- **A lawyer-facing packet keys its folders on the main `row_uid`, chosen as the lowest uid in the group — never on `project`.** An article whose four citations span four projects would otherwise name a different folder depending on which row the build started from. Identity fields come from the group, but `tier` / `section` / `page` / `quote` come from **each row's own `cites_id`**: GLAD being in Methods says nothing about where GlycoGlyph appears. `folder_uid` is not `is_primary_copy` — the latter picks which duplicate carries the exhibit highlight, the former only names a folder.
- **A timeline set stays in one folder, in numeric-prefix order.** Heras's preprint, its bioRxiv page and the 2024 article exist to show one argument against the filing date; splitting them by row scatters it. The plain file listing is alphabetical, so `article` sorts before `preprint` and hides the point — hence `01-preprint-…`, `02-biorxiv-page-…`, `03-article-…`. Copy the bytes without renaming: a renamed or re-saved PDF is harder to tie back to its master.
- **The 19 PDFs in `Notable Citations in Original Application` were already submitted and must not be counted again.** `tools/build-original-application-list.js` renders `Original-Application-Citations.md` in that folder; measured 2026-11-06, **18 matched a catalog row** on first-author surname + initials + year and **17 already carry a highlighted independent row**, so re-filing them would present the same evidence twice. One is `DEPENDENT`, not independent: `13_2023_Blood_S C Wu` is `cit-000506`, which OpenAlex resolves against the PI as an author.
- **A file name is weak evidence of identity, so print the basis.** `tools/build-original-application-list.js` matches on the *first-author* surname because Scholar truncates a byline after ~3 names, and reports surname-only matches as needing a person rather than folding them in. Journal/author boundary is inconsistent in the names (`J Med Chem_M N Stadtmueller` vs `Biochemistry R Billur`).
- **A "near miss" note must name an actual spelling difference.** The renderer used to flag a candidate surname that matched as an exact substring, printing "`van` in the name vs `van` in the document" — a note that says nothing. Require at least one edit and prefer the longest differing candidate.
- **A `Set` has `.size`, not `.length`, and nothing fails when you use the wrong one.** It made the inventory report "6 of NaN PDFs". When a generated sentence contains a count, read the rendered number, not just the exit code.
- **Never write a commit-message file with PowerShell's `Set-Content -Encoding utf8`** — it prepends a BOM, and `git commit -F` then puts U+FEFF in the subject line, which shows as `﻿Fetch the…` in `git log`. Write the message with the edit/create tool, or strip the BOM with node before committing. (Same root cause as the `Get-Content`/`Set-Content` rule below; hit again on 2026-11-08 on the RSC commit, fixed by `--amend`.)
- **Never rewrite a file in this repo with `Get-Content` + `Set-Content`.** On this machine `Get-Content` decodes UTF-8 as the ANSI codepage, so a read-modify-write round-trip mangles every em dash into `â€”` and `Set-Content -Encoding utf8` prepends a BOM — done to this file on 2026-11-06, turning a 13-line addition into a 63-insert/50-delete diff. The damage is *mixed*: text inserted later by the edit tool stays correct, so a whole-file un-mojibake pass rejects itself. Either edit with the edit tool, or rewrite through `node -e` with `fs.readFileSync(p,'utf8')`. Check `git diff --numstat` after any bulk text substitution — an addition should show deletions of `0`.

## OpenAlex Bulk Export (`OpenAlex/`)

- `OpenAlex/` at the repository root holds two CSVs the user exported on 2026-11-05 with the OQL desktop tool (`get articles since 2020 with (glycan OR glycosylation) in the title or abstract`, and `get works since 2020 in the topic [Glycosylation and Glycoproteins Research] (T10602)`). It is **reference material for a separate line of enquiry, not part of the evidence packet**: no tool in `tools/` reads it, and nothing in the ledger, store, dashboard or exhibits depends on it. Do not let a bulk export become a basis for an independence call — Google Scholar stays primary and corroboration goes per-row through `tools/crosscheck.js`, per the rules above.
- **There is no DOI column and no OpenAlex work id.** The columns are exactly `Title, Author, Year, Citation count, Open access`.
